claims.text: A calibrated heat treatment can induce a dual-phase microstructure containing well-dispersed nanoscale intermetallic precipitates in the lightweight high-entropy alloy.
The induced dual-phase microstructure will increase mechanical strength relative to the homogeneous single-phase state.
The induced dual-phase microstructure will improve corrosion resistance relative to the homogeneous single-phase state.
The induced dual-phase microstructure will improve high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to the homogeneous single-phase state.
The baseline alloy has a homogeneous single-phase structure and low density.
A suitable heat-treatment temperature window can promote fine-precipitate nucleation and growth while avoiding coarsening or dissolution.
Precipitate size, distribution, and interfacial coherency govern the proposed property improvements.
Nanoscale intermetallic precipitates impede dislocation motion and thereby strengthen the alloy.
Nanoscale intermetallic precipitates act as physical barriers to diffusion of corrosive species.
Nanoscale intermetallic precipitates act as physical barriers to oxygen diffusion.
The dual-phase alloy will exhibit a statistically significant increase in yield strength.
The dual-phase alloy will exhibit a statistically significant reduction in corrosion rate.
The dual-phase alloy will exhibit a reduced oxidation rate, represented by a thinner or more stable oxide layer.
The heat-treated alloy will maintain low density while its mechanical and environmental properties improve.
Precipitate coarsening, dissolution, or inhomogeneous distribution will eliminate the proposed benefits.
The proposed benefits will not occur if the alloy composition cannot support stable dual-phase formation.
The magnitude of the property changes depends on heat-treatment parameters and alloy composition.
Identically composed heat-treated and untreated samples provide a controlled comparison of the dual-phase and homogeneous states.
Failure to obtain statistically significant improvements in strength, corrosion resistance, and oxidation behavior would falsify the proposed joint-benefit hypothesis.
Failure to form a beneficial precipitate dispersion would falsify the hypothesis.
